title: Surface fastening and concealed services
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government, Electrical licences and credentials (last updated 23 June 2026); NSW Government, Plumbing, draining and gasfitting (last updated 31 July 2026; page metadata shows a later modified date); Queensland Building and Construction Commission, When you need a QBCC licence (last reviewed 11 August 2021); Building and Plumbing Commission (Victoria), Gasfitting work (last updated 30 June 2026).
audience: Handyman workers, deck and fence maintenance workers, and flat-pack and fixture installers
learningOutcomes: Choose a fixing suited to the substrate, the load and the finish.
Locate studs, joists and concealed services before drilling or fixing.
Stop and refer when a concealed service is found or suspected.

instruction.heading: Match the fixing to the substrate and the load
instruction.body: A fixing that holds in one material can fail in another. Timber framing takes screws into the stud or noggin. Plasterboard needs a fixing that spreads the load across the board, or a fixing that locates a stud. Masonry needs a masonry anchor of the correct size for the material and the depth. Hollow walls and cavity walls need fixings rated for hollow substrates, and the rating should come from the fixing manufacturer. Estimate the load before you fix anything: a shelf with a load on it, a grab rail, or a wall-mounted fixture carries force that must reach solid structure. If you cannot confirm the substrate or the load path, do not proceed on assumption.

instruction.heading: Locate studs, joists and services before drilling
instruction.body: Use a stud finder, a detector, and a visual check of the wall, including skirting, switch and power point positions, and the line of pipes beneath sinks. Concealed electrical cables often run vertically above and beside switches and power points, and horizontally at set heights, but a cable can be run in any direction. Do not rely on the position of a single outlet as proof of where cables run. Mark the wall with the located positions and confirm before you drill. If a detector gives an unclear reading, stop and use a different location or refer.

instruction.heading: Stop and refer when a service is found
instruction.body: If you find or suspect a concealed electrical, gas or water service, stop drilling or fixing in that area. Do not move or cut the service. Record the location, the time and what was observed, and refer the work to a licensed trade. Continue with other fixings only where the wall has been confirmed clear and the approver agrees. Fixing into a service is a common cause of injury and of costly damage (UNCONFIRMED: no source is cited for this statement), and it is also work that falls under licensed trade boundaries, as set out for the states checked in this course (see “Electrical boundaries and referral” and “Water, plumbing and gas boundaries”).

instruction.heading: Everyday fixings and the state position
instruction.body: Everyday fixings such as towel rails, shelves and grab rails are taught here so that you can match the fixing to the substrate and the load, and locate services first. The cited pages do not set a state licence rule for the fixing itself. The licence rule applies when a concealed service is found or disturbed. In New South Wales, a licence or certificate is needed for wiring work regardless of the cost of the work, except for equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC, and a licence or certificate is needed for plumbing, draining or gasfitting work at any cost, so a concealed service found there must be referred to a licensed worker. In Queensland, a QBCC licence is needed for plumbing, drainage and gas fitting at any value (see Water, plumbing and gas boundaries), and the Queensland electrical position is not in this lesson's sources, so a suspected concealed cable must be referred. In Victoria, the gasfitting definition covers items (see Water, plumbing and gas boundaries), and the Victorian electrical and water positions are not confirmed in this lesson's sources, so a suspected concealed service must be referred.

procedure: Identify the substrate, the fixing type and the load, and write them down.
Choose a fixing rated for the substrate and the load from the manufacturer data.
Locate studs, joists and services with a detector and a visual check.
Mark the located positions and confirm them before drilling.
Drill only in confirmed clear positions, with the correct bit and depth.
If a service is found or suspected, stop, do not move it, record it, and refer.
Test the fixing with a controlled load before it is relied on.

workedExamples.situation: A heavy towel rail is to be fixed to plasterboard, and the detector gives an unclear reading near the planned fixing point.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the fixing go ahead in the planned position?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. An unclear reading means the wall cannot be confirmed clear. Move to a confirmed stud or use a fixing rated for the load, after the position is confirmed. If the reading suggests a service, stop and refer. A towel rail carries an ongoing load, so it needs a fixing that reaches solid structure.

equipmentAndPpe: Drill, bits and drivers matched to the fixing
Fixings rated for the substrate and the load, with manufacturer data
Torch for checking under sinks and behind fixtures

commonErrors.error: Using a plastic wall plug in plasterboard for a heavy load.
commonErrors.prevention: Match the fixing to the substrate and the load, using the manufacturer rating.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a cable runs only where the switch or outlet is.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a detector and visual checks, and refer if the location is unclear.

commonErrors.error: Moving or cutting a service to reach the fixing position.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, do not move the service, record it and refer.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Finding or disturbing a concealed electrical service requires referral to a licensed electrical worker. In New South Wales, a licence or certificate is needed for wiring work whatever the cost, except for equipment at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC (electrical page, last updated 23 June 2026). This lesson grants no electrical licence.

Finding or disturbing a concealed gas or water service requires referral to a licensed plumber or gasfitter (course guidance). The NSW plumbing page (last updated 31 July 2026) sets the licence requirements for plumbing, draining and gasfitting work. Licence positions are recorded in “Water, plumbing and gas boundaries”.

Queensland and Victoria: the electrical licence positions for concealed cables are not stated in this lesson's cited sources. Refer any suspected concealed cable in those states and do not treat the work as licence-free.
Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: The substrate, the load and the fixing are recorded before any fixing is made.
Fixing positions are confirmed clear by at least one method before drilling.
Any suspected service is stopped, recorded and referred before work continues in that area.
documentationEvidence: Fixing record with the substrate, the load and the fixing type
Service-location record with the method used and any referral
summary: Match the fixing to the substrate and to the load, using the manufacturer rating.
Locate studs and services before drilling, and do not rely on a single outlet to show where cables run.
Stop and refer if a service is found or suspected.

knowledgeChecks.question: A detector gives an unclear reading at the planned fixing point. What should you do?
options: Treat the wall as unknown, move to a known position or refer, and do not drill blind
Drill anyway because the reading is probably wrong and the wall is fine
Use a longer screw, since it will reach past any hidden service in the wall
Ask the client to decide where the fixing goes, since they know the wall best

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the correct action if you find a concealed cable while drilling?
options: Cut it and reconnect it with a joiner, then carry on with the fixing in the same row
Stop, do not move or cut it, record it, and refer to a licensed electrical worker
Tape it well and continue with the fixing in the same place today, since the tape holds
Continue with the fixing in another row, since the cable is not in that row

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a fixing be matched to the load?
options: So the fixing looks neat and tidy on the surface of the wall once it is done
Because manufacturers require it for warranty only and nothing else
So the load is carried into solid structure and the fixing does not fail
To reduce the number of fixings used on the job and save on hardware
